article_title: Classworks Math
citation: Classworks Individualized Learning. (2022). Evidence summary. https://www.classworks.com
title: Individualized learning unit pattern: direct instruction, applied activities, and formative mastery check
description: Each Classworks instructional unit follows a recurring structure: "direct instruction, activities to apply learning, and a short formative test focused on strengthening a specific skill." Direct instruction comes in two-to-three-minute segments teachers can also use in classrooms, extended learning takes the form of interactive games and activities that differentiate by instructional strategies, and a formative assessment confirms mastery. Students encounter varied instructional approaches, interactivity types, and degrees of games versus concrete instruction as they learn each skill.
requirements: Assessment data from which to generate the Individualized Learning Path
constraints: Units target one specific skill at a time
target_learners: K-12 students in tiered intervention
target_learning_goals: Mastery of specific skills
examples: Classworks units pair two-to-three-minute direct-instruction segments with interactive games and a short formative test per skill
key_sources: Classworks Individualized Learning. (2022). Evidence summary. https://www.classworks.com

article_title: The Instructional Leadership Corps: Teachers Leading Sustainable Professional Learning in Their Communities
citation: Lotan, R. A., & Burns, D. (2019). The Instructional Leadership Corps: Teachers leading sustainable professional learning in their communities. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/instructional-leadership-corps-teachers-leading
title: Iterative multisession professional development workshops with classroom application between sessions
description: Professional development workshops (PDWs) are a hallmark of the ILC. The pattern provides multiple learning sessions separated by opportunities for teachers to design and apply new strategies in their classrooms; the report states this is "a key element in helping teachers make lasting changes in instructional practice," in contrast to single-session workshops after which teachers may return to familiar practices. In the first workshop, participants experience instructional strategies and collaboratively plan lessons; in the second, they analyze student work samples, reflect, and exchange feedback for iterative improvement.
requirements: Multiple sessions separated by classroom application opportunities
Collaborative teams so teachers will attempt new approaches and refine them with feedback and practice
constraints: Follow-up involving modeling or observation-and-feedback of participant teachers is rare but important
target_learners: Practicing K-12 teachers implementing new standards
target_learning_goals: Sustained, standards-aligned changes in classroom instructional practice
examples: In the first of two consecutive workshops, participants experience strategies, study concrete examples often with videotapes of practice, and plan lessons; in the second they analyze student work artifacts
key_sources: Lotan, R. A., & Burns, D. (2019). The Instructional Leadership Corps: Teachers leading sustainable professional learning in their communities. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/instructional-leadership-corps-teachers-leading

article_title: The Instructional Leadership Corps: Entrusting Professional Learning in the Hands of the Profession
citation: Lotan, R. A., Burns, D., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2019). The Instructional Leadership Corps: Entrusting professional learning in the hands of the profession. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/instructional-leadership-corps-professional-learning
title: The ILC iterative professional development workshop model: multiple sessions separated by classroom application, reflection, and refinement
description: The ILC's hallmark is a sequence of professional development workshops (PDWs) in which teacher leaders demonstrate instructional shifts, support colleagues in trying new practices, and reconvene to analyze results. In the first of two consecutive workshops, "participants experience—rather than just observe—instructional strategies designed to deepen student learning" and collaboratively plan lessons; in the second, participants analyze student work samples, reflect, and exchange feedback for iterative improvement. This contrasts with single-session workshops after which teachers may return to familiar practices.
requirements: Teacher leaders trained in the instructional shifts; multiple learning sessions separated by opportunities for teachers to design and apply new strategies in their classrooms
constraints: The report notes meaningful follow-up was important but rare, and that achieving depth versus reach is a perennial dilemma in teacher professional learning initiatives
target_learners: Practicing K-12 teachers
Site-based administrators
target_learning_goals: Implementing CCSS and NGSS instructional shifts
Sustained change in classroom instructional practice
examples: Two consecutive workshops in which teachers plan a lesson addressing an instructional shift, then return to analyze student work and refine practice
key_sources: Lotan, R. A., Burns, D., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2019). The Instructional Leadership Corps: Entrusting professional learning in the hands of the profession. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/instructional-leadership-corps-professional-learning

article_title: The Instructional Leadership Corps: Entrusting Professional Learning in the Hands of the Profession
citation: Lotan, R. A., Burns, D., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2019). The Instructional Leadership Corps: Entrusting professional learning in the hands of the profession. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/instructional-leadership-corps-professional-learning
title: The ILC 'teachers teaching teachers' model of teacher-led, systemically connected professional learning
description: The ILC is a statewide collaborative in which expert teachers, trained through statewide and regional conferences, organize local professional development to spark iterative changes in practice. Its "purposeful approach" of "teachers teaching teachers" empowers teachers to lead sustainable professional development and advance instructional capacity within their districts. The model replaces one-shot outside-consultant workshops with ongoing, locally led learning, and its theory of action resonates with Jaquith's framework for enhancing instructional capacity, which calls for opportunities to develop professional knowledge, resources, recognition of instructional expertise, and organizational structures supporting collaboration and trust.
requirements: A corps of trained teacher leaders selected for instructional expertise and leadership, organized in local teams
Institutional partners providing guidance, resources, network upkeep, and recognition
constraints: The report notes practitioner-led professional learning has often failed where teacher leaders are appointed but not integrated into the work of the schools
target_learners: Practicing K-12 teachers
Teacher leaders
Site and district administrators
target_learning_goals: Implementing new standards-aligned instruction
Building district instructional capacity and teacher leadership
examples: Four case studies: Madera USD (language development), Conejo Valley USD (science alignment), East Side Alliance (standards-based mathematics), and North Orange County/CSU Fullerton (Teachers Teaching Teachers conferences)
key_sources: Lotan, R. A., Burns, D., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2019). The Instructional Leadership Corps: Entrusting professional learning in the hands of the profession. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/instructional-leadership-corps-professional-learning

article_title: High-Quality Early Childhood Assessment: Learning from States' Use of Kindergarten Entry Assessments
citation: Yun, C., Melnick, H., & Wechsler, M. (2021). High-quality early childhood assessment: Learning from states' use of kindergarten entry assessments. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/high-quality-kea
title: Illinois KIDS: a statewide observational KEA based on the DRDP-K with mandatory professional development
description: Illinois has used the Kindergarten Individual Development Survey statewide since 2017; the report calls it 'the most populous state in the United States to require a comprehensive KEA.' KIDS is based on the DRDP-K, and of three assessment versions only the shortest, the State Readiness Measures, is required, including 14 items measuring approaches to learning, social and emotional learning, language and literacy, and mathematics. Scores are based on teacher observation over multiple authentic activities in children's natural classroom settings. The state provides mandatory implementation workshops with substitutes, tailored coaching, and an annual summit, and publishes aggregated state-level KEA data annually.
requirements: Mandatory implementation workshops, with substitutes provided so teachers can attend
constraints: Only the shortest version, the State Readiness Measures with 14 items, is required for Illinois districts
target_learners: kindergarten children in Illinois public schools
target_learning_goals: informing kindergarten instruction and facilitating communication with families
examples: The Illinois State Board of Education publishes aggregated state-level KEA data annually, which have informed policy conversations about expanding access to early learning
key_sources: Yun, C., Melnick, H., & Wechsler, M. (2021). High-quality early childhood assessment: Learning from states' use of kindergarten entry assessments. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/high-quality-kea

article_title: An Overview of State Financial Aid in Illinois, Indiana, and Minnesota
citation: Victoria Jackson. (2025). An Overview of State Financial Aid in Illinois, Indiana, and Minnesota. EdTrust. https://edtrust.org
title: Illinois Monetary Award Program (MAP) grant
description: MAP is Illinois's largest and main need-based grant, with no merit requirements and eligibility via FAFSA or an alternative application for undocumented students; the report's Table 3 shows it meets nine of ten framework metrics. It functions "similarly to a first dollar award" and is prorated by credit hours, with a 2024-25 maximum award of $8,400. MAP spending was $595.9 million, or 98.8% of Illinois's $603.2 million undergraduate state aid in 2022-23.
requirements: Students must demonstrate financial need; those with a Student Aid Index above 9,000 are ineligible
constraints: Students who are incarcerated are not eligible for aid; students in default are also marked ineligible in the analysis table
target_learners: Illinois residents with financial need
recent high school graduates
adult learners
undocumented students
target_learning_goals: affording in-state postsecondary education
examples: Awards are first-come, first-served by FAFSA submission date, with a priority deadline for returning recipients
key_sources: Victoria Jackson. (2025). An Overview of State Financial Aid in Illinois, Indiana, and Minnesota. EdTrust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED678857

article_title: School network reorganization under educational and spatial constraints using classical and quantum optimization
citation: Alessia Ciacco, Luigi Di Puglia Pugliese, Francesca Guerriero. (2026). School network reorganization under educational and spatial constraints using classical and quantum optimization. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05427
title: An ILP optimization framework for school network aggregation under institutional, territorial, and accessibility constraints
description: The article proposes an Integer Linear Programming model for regional school network reorganization in the Italian context. As the authors state, it "jointly incorporates institutional compatibility, administrative regulations, school aggregation decisions, road-network travel-time accessibility, territorial fragility, and school capacity constraints." The model decides which autonomous school institutions retain administrative autonomy as hubs and which are aggregated into them, without closing physical facilities. It is framed as addressing the aggregation component of reorganization, not end-to-end planning including closure or transport.
requirements: Institutional, territorial, and demographic data on schools, including enrollments, road-network travel times, and territorial criticality levels
A policy parameter defining the minimum proportion of schools that must remain active
constraints: The article states the model "does not constitute a complete end-to-end school network reorganization model including all possible planning decisions, such as school opening or closure, facility relocation, capacity expansion, transport planning, multi-period demographic evolution, or budget allocation"
target_learners: school-age students in regional school networks
target_learning_goals: maintaining adequate educational service provision and accessibility across territories during school network reorganization
key_sources: Alessia Ciacco, Luigi Di Puglia Pugliese, Francesca Guerriero. (2026). School network reorganization under educational and spatial constraints using classical and quantum optimization. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05427

article_title: Online peer assessment: effects of cognitive and affective feedback
citation: Jingyan Lu, Nancy Law. (2012). Online peer assessment: effects of cognitive and affective feedback. Instructional Science 40:257–275. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-011-9177-2
title: iLAP (Interactive Learning and Assessment Platform)
description: iLAP is an online learning platform developed to support teaching and assessment of Liberal Studies in Hong Kong schools. Its functions are fourfold: "assignment submission, rubric development, assessment implementation, and performance monitoring". Its peer assessment interface comprises a rubric area, where students assign scores via drop-down menus across criteria and quality levels, and a comment area for free-text feedback; grades and comments become immediately available to assessees.
requirements: Teachers create or adopt assessment rubrics specifying task dimensions and rating criteria for varying levels of performance
constraints: In this study assessment activities were not compulsory and students could choose which subtasks to assess
target_learners: secondary two (13- to 14-year-old) students in Hong Kong
target_learning_goals: inquiry-based Liberal Studies project work
examples: Students in groups of four or five reviewed group members' individual assignments across five project subtasks using teacher-assigned rubrics
key_sources: Jingyan Lu, Nancy Law. (2012). Online peer assessment: effects of cognitive and affective feedback. Instructional Science 40:257–275. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-011-9177-2

article_title: A Learning Patterns Perspective on Student Learning in Higher Education: State of the Art and Moving Forward
citation: Jan D. Vermunt & Vincent Donche. (2017). A Learning Patterns Perspective on Student Learning in Higher Education: State of the Art and Moving Forward. Educ Psychol Rev 29:269–299. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9414-6
title: Inventory of Learning Styles (ILS) measuring four components of student learning patterns
description: The ILS is the self-report instrument developed by Vermunt (1996, 1998) to measure the four components of student learning patterns on a larger scale: processing strategies (deep, stepwise, concrete), regulation strategies (self-regulation, external regulation, lack of regulation), conceptions of learning, and learning orientations. Its name was kept after the 2004 renaming of 'style' to 'pattern' to avoid confusion, though the authors note Inventory of Learning Patterns would have been a better name. A strong point is that "it was grounded in interview research with the target student population about their learning in natural, real-life settings".
requirements: Used with populations whose learning in natural, real-life settings informed its development; self-report instruments have limitations that should be matched to the purpose of measurement
constraints: As a self-report instrument it has limitations shared with other methods; the name retains 'styles' although the concept was renamed 'learning pattern'
target_learners: university and higher education students
target_learning_goals: measuring students' processing strategies, regulation strategies, conceptions of learning, and learning orientations
examples: The review's systematic search retained 44 learning pattern studies in which the ILS was used between 2004 and 2016
key_sources: Jan D. Vermunt & Vincent Donche. (2017). A Learning Patterns Perspective on Student Learning in Higher Education: State of the Art and Moving Forward. Educ Psychol Rev 29:269–299. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9414-6

article_title: Intensive Longitudinal Methods in School Research: A Systematic Literature Review
citation: Carina Schreiber & Michael Becker. (2026). Intensive Longitudinal Methods in School Research: A Systematic Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10203-x
title: Comprehensive checklist of reporting criteria for intensive longitudinal studies
description: The review offers "a comprehensive checklist of reporting criteria for intensive longitudinal methods", integrating the APA Journal Article Reporting Standards, the Trull and Ebner-Priemer (2020) guidelines, and the review's own findings. The checklist covers sample justification, sampling scheme and scheduling, item text and psychometrics, hardware and software, compliance procedures, valid and missing data, the final dataset, analysis preparation, and analysis details. It is operationalised in Table 2, where each criterion was coded met or not met per article.
requirements: Researchers should justify sample and sample size (e.g., using multilevel power analyses) and give rationales for sampling scheme, assessment frequency, and questionnaire density
constraints: Adherence rates for the majority of guidelines were questionably low even among articles published in the past five years
target_learners: school researchers designing intensive longitudinal studies
target_learning_goals: transparent, replicable reporting of intensive longitudinal study methods
examples: The review coded each of the 257 included articles against the checklist criteria, e.g., reporting full text of response options was met by 92.2% of articles, while justifying sample size was met by only 4.7%
key_sources: Carina Schreiber & Michael Becker. (2026). Intensive Longitudinal Methods in School Research: A Systematic Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10203-x

article_title: Intensive Longitudinal Methods in School Research: A Systematic Literature Review
citation: Carina Schreiber & Michael Becker. (2026). Intensive Longitudinal Methods in School Research: A Systematic Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10203-x
title: Methodological parameter framework for designing intensive longitudinal studies
description: The review organises the design of intensive longitudinal studies around core methodological parameters: study duration, assessment frequency, sampling scheme (fixed, random, semi-random, event-based), item phrasing and questionnaire density, and data-collection device. It argues these choices "contain, rather implicitly, theoretical assumptions about the psychological processes under investigation and delimit the kinds of inferences that can be drawn from the data", requiring alignment between parameters, research questions, and constructs. For example, low-frequency assessments implicitly assume no meaningful within-day fluctuations.
requirements: Methodological decisions should be explicitly justified in light of the specific research questions, theoretical assumptions, and study populations under investigation
Assessment frequency should be balanced with study duration to keep participant burden acceptable while generating sufficient data points
constraints: Established validated trait-level measures are usually too long and retrospective, so researchers often must adapt or develop state-level instruments, which may alter the construct measured
Time-varying confounders and lagged effects remain an issue for within-person causal inference
target_learners: school researchers
students and teachers as study participants
target_learning_goals: capturing within-person fluctuations in students' and teachers' experiences, emotions, cognitions, and behaviours in everyday school life
examples: The review illustrates the framework with a hypothetical study of students' motivation, showing how different parameter specifications yield fundamentally different insights
key_sources: Carina Schreiber & Michael Becker. (2026). Intensive Longitudinal Methods in School Research: A Systematic Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10203-x

article_title: Patterns in Student Learning: Relationships Between Learning Strategies, Conceptions of Learning, and Learning Orientations
citation: Vermunt, J. D. & Vermetten, Y. J. (2004). Patterns in Student Learning: Relationships Between Learning Strategies, Conceptions of Learning, and Learning Orientations. Educational Psychology Review. https://dspacelibrary.uu.nl/handle/1874/11958
title: Inventory of Learning Styles (ILS): 120-item diagnostic questionnaire covering processing, regulation, conceptions, and orientations
description: The ILS is a diagnostic instrument developed from phenomenographic interview analyses and factor, reliability, item, and test-retest analyses. "The final version of the ILS consists of 120 statements that cover four learning components: cognitive processing strategies, metacognitive regulation strategies, conceptions of learning, and learning orientations." It assesses five scales in each component, rated on 5-point scales, and has been used in at least ten countries since 1992.
requirements: Administration to students able to report on their own study behavior; adapted language and school context for younger or non-Dutch populations
constraints: Regulation-strategy scales showed lower internal consistencies (alphas from .48) in some regular-university samples
target_learners: higher education students
secondary education students (adapted version)
target_learning_goals: diagnosis of learning strategies, conceptions, and orientations
examples: Used in studies across the Netherlands, Belgium, Finland, England, Cyprus, USA, Brazil, Argentina, Indonesia, and Sri Lanka
key_sources: Vermunt, J. D. & Vermetten, Y. J. (2004). Patterns in Student Learning: Relationships Between Learning Strategies, Conceptions of Learning, and Learning Orientations. Educational Psychology Review. https://dspacelibrary.uu.nl/handle/1874/11958

article_title: Using Ontological Engineering to Overcome AI-ED Problems: Contribution, Impact and Perspectives
citation: Mizoguchi, R., & Bourdeau, J. (2015). Using Ontological Engineering to Overcome AI-ED Problems: Contribution, Impact and Perspectives. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0077-5
title: I_L event: a concept unifying learning and instructional events, formed 'in the wild'
description: During collaborative ontology engineering for OMNIBUS, the authors lacked a concept for what happens when a learning agent and an instruction agent act and interact together. They created the I_L event, "which integrates a 'Learning_event' with an 'Instructional_event' in one entity, and represents interaction between the learner and the instructional agent, as well as the activity on each respective side". The article frames this as an instance of Engeström and Sannino's concept formation in the wild, and notes the term itself needs improvement for human sharing.
requirements: Connection to a top-level ontology, which constrained concept formation during its creation
constraints: The authors state the term 'I_L event' needs improvement to be shared effectively among humans
target_learners: Ontology engineers and AIED system builders
target_learning_goals: Representing learning and instruction jointly in ontologies for authoring systems
examples: The authors also created the What_to_learn concept out of necessity, to express anything being learned intentionally or not
key_sources: Mizoguchi, R., & Bourdeau, J. (2015). Using Ontological Engineering to Overcome AI-ED Problems: Contribution, Impact and Perspectives. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0077-5

article_title: How to Improve the Explanatory Power of an Intelligent Textbook: a Case Study in Legal Writing
citation: Sovrano Francesco, Ashley Kevin, Brusilovsky Peter Leonid, Vitali Fabio. (2024). How to Improve the Explanatory Power of an Intelligent Textbook: a Case Study in Legal Writing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00399-w
title: Illocutionary theory of explanation: explaining means answering an explicit question together with relevant implicit archetypal questions
description: Grounded in Achinstein's Ordinary Language Philosophy account, the article defines explaining as an illocutionary act: "Explaining is an illocutionary act that provides answers to an explicit question on some topic along with answers to several other implicit or unformulated questions deemed necessary for the explainee to understand the topic properly." Implicit questions are instances of archetypes such as why, how, what, who, when, where, drawn from AMR and PDTB discourse theories. YAI4Edu operationalizes this by organizing textbook content as clusters of archetypal question-answer pairs.
requirements: A collection of texts that adequately answers a set of archetypal questions about the explanandum
In the generic case with no assumptions about the explainee, only archetypal questions can be exploited for illocution
constraints: Illocution was considered too abstract to implement directly; the article notes the computer-friendly interpretation relies on pre-defined archetypes
target_learners: English-speaking university students learning legal writing
target_learning_goals: Understanding complex textbook topics through question-driven explanations
examples: The article contrasts the non-explanatory answer "I am fine" with an answer that also addresses archetypal questions, which becomes an explanation
key_sources: Sovrano Francesco, Ashley Kevin, Brusilovsky Peter Leonid, Vitali Fabio. (2024). How to Improve the Explanatory Power of an Intelligent Textbook: a Case Study in Legal Writing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00399-w

article_title: Understanding teacher design practices for digital inquiry–based science learning: the case of Go-Lab
citation: de Jong, T., Gillet, D., Rodríguez-Triana, M. J., Hovardas, T., Dikke, D., Doran, R., Dziabenko, O., Koslowsky, J., Korventausta, M., Law, E., Pedaste, M., Tasiopoulou, E., Vidal, G., & Zacharia, Z. C. (2021). Understanding teacher design practices for digital inquiry–based science learning: the case of Go-Lab. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09904-z
title: Inquiry Learning Spaces (ILSs) as digital inquiry environments
description: Inquiry Learning Spaces are online or digital environments where students interact with learning material including labs, apps, and multimedia resources. Material is organized in phases following the Go-Lab inquiry cycle, which includes "orientation, conceptualization, investigation, conclusion, and discussion" phases. Teachers can adapt the number and names of phases, populate them with content, and configure apps to scaffold student inquiry processes such as hypothesis construction and experiment design.
requirements: An ILS requires a lab, apps, and multimedia material organized in inquiry cycle phases
target_learners: STEM students in primary and secondary education
target_learning_goals: Inquiry skills
Hypothesis construction
Experiment design

article_title: How pictures and graphs aid learning from print
citation: How Pictures and Graphs Aid Learning From Print. (1953). Audio-Visual Communication Review. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Audio-Visual+Communication+Review
title: University of Illinois Human Resources Research Institute Research Memo No. 11, How Pictures and Graphs Aid Learning From Print
description: A research memo produced by the University of Illinois Division of Communications' Human Resources Research Institute. Its purpose was "To summarize the main experimental studies on pictures and graphs as aids to learning from print," and its authors abstracted over 50 studies, stating it was safe to say most, if not all, experimental evidence on the problem had been reviewed. The memo identified neglected issues and summarized design conditions for effective pictures.
requirements: Abstracts experimental studies bearing on pictures and graphs as aids to learning from print
target_learners: learners studying from printed materials
target_learning_goals: learning from print-supported instruction
examples: The memo's results section lists unresolved questions such as whether graphs and pictures aid retention and who learns most from such aids

article_title: A study of motivations, behavior, and contributions quality in online communities of teachers: A data analytics approach
citation: Gutiérrez-Páez, N. F., Santos, P., Hernández-Leo, D., & Carrió, M. (2023). A study of motivations, behavior, and contributions quality in online communities of teachers: A data analytics approach. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104829
title: ILDE+ platform for online communities of pre-service teachers sharing learning designs
description: ILDE+ is a customized version of the Integrated Learning Design Environment supporting an online community of pre-service teachers who explore, share, discuss, and co-create learning designs. It implements six main functionalities including an LD creation template with metadata, commenting, design duplication preserving authorship, co-design via shared authorship, and social features such as "a like button for the designs, counters of visualizations and comments, or follow button for the members of the community." The platform logs user actions for analytics.
requirements: Users must register on the platform to access its functionalities
constraints: The platform was studied in the early stages of the community, when comments and likes were rarely used
target_learners: pre-service science teachers in a master's degree program
target_learning_goals: collaborative creation and peer review of learning designs
examples: Used across two editions of a Biology teaching course in a pre-service teacher master's program

article_title: Effects of Cloze Instructional Approach on Senior Secondary School Students' Achievement in Igbo Language Reading Comprehension
citation: Nneka Justina Eze. (2015). Effects of Cloze Instructional Approach on Senior Secondary School Students' Achievement in Igbo Language Reading Comprehension. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.21. http://www.iiste.org
title: Igbo Language Reading Comprehension Test (ILRCT)
description: The Igbo Language Reading Comprehension Test (ILRCT) was the outcome instrument for the study, containing five comprehension passages drawn from Igbo Language Literature books including Isi Akwu dara n's ala, Uwadiegwu, and Okpa aku eri eri. It was validated by specialists in Igbo language and Measurement and Evaluation for relevance, general test format, suitability and clarity. Reliability was assessed by test-retest with Pearson's Product Moment correlation, yielding a stability index of 0.72, and inter rater reliability using Kendal's W yielded an index of 0.67. The same passages were used for pretest and posttest, with passages reshuffled and different coloured papers to reduce memorization effects.
requirements: Validated by specialists in Igbo language and Measurement and Evaluation
constraints: The same comprehension passages were used for pretest and posttest, requiring reshuffled passage order and different coloured papers to eliminate errors of memorization of previous passages
target_learners: Senior Secondary Class 1 students of Igbo language
target_learning_goals: Igbo language reading comprehension achievement
examples: Used to collect pretest and posttest data from 89 students in two intact classes in Abakaliki education zone
key_sources: Nneka Justina Eze. (2015). Effects of Cloze Instructional Approach on Senior Secondary School Students' Achievement in Igbo Language Reading Comprehension. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.21. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1079076

article_title: A Study of Multimedia Application-Based Vocabulary Acquisition
citation: Jing Shao. (2012). A Study of Multimedia Application-based Vocabulary Acquisition. English Language Teaching, 5(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n10p202
title: I Love English Vocabulary (ILEV) multimedia vocabulary software
description: The instrument applied in the research is the software I Love English Vocabulary (ILEV), produced by Beijing Wrestler Computer Technology Company Ltd. The article states it is "the widely used vocabulary software program in China" and that "The software is used to assist word input, word retention and word use." It served as the multimedia application-based instruction for the 40-student experimental group.
requirements: Requires learners to have computer-operating skills, which the article says many students lack
constraints: The study examined only this one multimedia program, so it cannot include all multimedia language learning applications
target_learners: Chinese college freshmen EFL learners
target_learning_goals: vocabulary input, retention and use
key_sources: Jing Shao. (2012). A Study of Multimedia Application-based Vocabulary Acquisition. English Language Teaching, 5(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n10p202

article_title: Understanding the Integrated Learning Course Model: "Academic Transition to Tertiary Education"
citation: David R. Arendale. (2014). Understanding the Integrated Learning Course Model: Academic Transition to Tertiary Education. International Journal of Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.5430/ijhe.v3n4p1
title: Linked-course learning community pattern integrating study strategies with companion course content
description: The pattern pairs a content course with a support course that meets twice weekly and uses the same textbook, readings, and materials, so study strategies are applied directly to actual course work. Sessions mix "short lectures, group discussions, small group assignments, and other educational activities," and enrollment is capped at 24 to create a small-class experience within large first-year courses. The article situates this within learning communities' linked-courses practice, which it reports leads to higher student learning outcomes.
requirements: Concurrent enrollment in both the content course and the IL course
Use of the same course materials as the target class for direct application
constraints: Offered only where the course professor is supportive of the program
target_learners: First-year tertiary students in academically-challenging gatekeeper courses
target_learning_goals: Effective textbook reading and note taking
Peer collaboration and learning networks
Application of course content
examples: IL class sessions use the target course's textbook and assigned readings, with instructor-created handouts and quizzes added

article_title: Understanding the Integrated Learning Course Model: "Academic Transition to Tertiary Education"
citation: David R. Arendale. (2014). Understanding the Integrated Learning Course Model: Academic Transition to Tertiary Education. International Journal of Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.5430/ijhe.v3n4p1
title: Ten key success factors for sustaining a linked academic-support course, including weekly faculty contact and targeting high-risk courses
description: Based on more than four decades of IL courses at UMN, the article lists factors it considers key to success: the IL instructor "knows what goes on during the target content class by meeting with the faculty member weekly," ongoing professional development occurs, IL is offered only with supportive professors, outcomes are evaluated each term, targeted classes show 30 percent or more D/F/withdrawal grades, cooperative learning fosters a learning community, and efficacy reports sustain stakeholder support. Resources include a dedicated classroom, media projection, photocopying, and an instructor salary sufficient to attract graduate students with prior teaching experience.
requirements: Salary sufficient to attract graduate students with prior teaching experience
A supportive academic department to host the IL course and mentor the instructional component
TRIO director time for selection, training, observing, coaching, and evaluating the program
constraints: Per-student cost of approximately $130 assumes class size capped at 24 and flat-rate tuition at 13 or more credit hours

target_learning_goals: Academic achievement in gatekeeper courses
Sustained institutional support for academic support programs
examples: The TRIO SSS director holds a one-day training workshop before fall term and meets periodically with IL instructors during the term

article_title: The Enhancement of Mathematical Critical Thinking Ability of Aliyah Madrasas Student Model Using Gorontalo by Interactive Learning Setting Cooperative Model
citation: Husnaeni. (2016). The Enhancement of Mathematical Critical Thinking Ability of Aliyah Madrasas Student Model Using Gorontalo by Interactive Learning Setting Cooperative Model. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(8). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1099553
title: Interactive Learning Setting Cooperative Model (ILSC/SSIPs) as an instructional framework for mathematical critical thinking
description: The ILSC model (also called SSIPs) is an interactive learning model with cooperative settings that emphasizes students constructing knowledge through problem solving in groups. It rests on four principles: "cooperation; freedom of expression; responsibility to yourself and groups; and equality". The model follows five syntax phases: introduction, activity or problem solving, presentation and discussion, closing, and assessment (before and after learning). It is designed to maximize interaction between teachers, students, and material.
requirements: Teachers must facilitate student interaction with students so that teaching and learning activities can take place properly
Assessment is done before and after learning
constraints: The model requires active students and was studied in the context of Aliyah Madrasas (Islamic senior secondary) mathematics classes
target_learners: Grade X (senior secondary) students in Aliyah Madrasas
target_learning_goals: Mathematical critical thinking ability across five aspects: trigger event, exploration, drawing conclusions, clarification, and resolution
examples: In the study, teachers organized classes into groups, conveyed ranking groups, provided instructional materials, and led discussions where groups reported results and responded to other groups' opinions
key_sources: Husnaeni. (2016). The Enhancement of Mathematical Critical Thinking Ability of Aliyah Madrasas Student Model Using Gorontalo by Interactive Learning Setting Cooperative Model. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(8). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1095328

article_title: The Enhancement of Mathematical Critical Thinking Ability of Aliyah Madrasas Student Model Using Gorontalo by Interactive Learning Setting Cooperative Model
citation: Husnaeni. (2016). The Enhancement of Mathematical Critical Thinking Ability of Aliyah Madrasas Student Model Using Gorontalo by Interactive Learning Setting Cooperative Model. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(8). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1099553
title: Five-phase lesson structure for ILSC mathematics learning
description: The ILSC model follows a five-phase lesson syntax: (1) Introduction — organizing the class, conveying group rankings and materials, and explaining tasks; (2) Activity or problem solving — reminding students of prerequisite material and performing teacher-determined activities; (3) Presentation and discussion — groups report results, teacher leads discussion, other groups respond, and the teacher poses questions that allow students to think critically and connect models to symbolic representations; (4) Closing — re-examining what students did and learned, making summaries; (5) Assessment — conducted before and after learning.
requirements: Teachers must organize groups, convey rankings, provide materials, and structure the sequence of activities, presentation, and assessment
constraints: Assessment must occur both before and after learning to measure enhancement
target_learners: Secondary school students working in cooperative groups
target_learning_goals: Mathematical concept construction, critical thinking, and problem solving
examples: In the presentation phase, the teacher asks questions that allow students to think critically and connect the model to relevant symbolic representations

article_title: Eight practical strategies for designing case-based flipped learning to foster clinical reasoning in preclinical medical students.
citation: Si J. (2025). Eight practical strategies for designing case-based flipped learning to foster clinical reasoning in preclinical medical students. Annals of Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586874
title: Illness script theory as the knowledge-oriented foundation for clinical reasoning activities in case-based flipped learning
description: The article grounds flipped learning activities in illness script theory, under which clinical reasoning depends on structured knowledge structures. According to the article, illness scripts are "goal-directed knowledge structures that experienced clinicians use to interpret patient information and make clinical decisions" that "evolve through repeated integration of biomedical and clinical knowledge over time". For novices, the article prescribes first building foundational scripts and then refining them through applied practice with clinical cases, operationalised in a clinical reasoning worksheet that integrates illness script tables with differential diagnoses, enabling conditions, pathophysiological mechanisms, and clinical manifestations.
requirements: Instructional activities must explicitly guide students to construct and refine their own illness scripts rather than merely promoting engagement
constraints: Scripts build gradually: the article states novices begin with foundational illness scripts refined through repeated practice over time, so the theory supports progressive rather than one-off reasoning instruction
target_learners: Preclinical medical students with limited medical knowledge and clinical exposure
target_learning_goals: Clinical reasoning development
Construction of structured clinical knowledge (illness scripts)
examples: A clinical reasoning worksheet integrating an illness script table with differential diagnoses, enabling conditions, pathophysiological mechanisms, and clinical manifestations, used for in-class script construction
key_sources: Si J. (2025). Eight practical strategies for designing case-based flipped learning to foster clinical reasoning in preclinical medical students. Annals of Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586874

article_title: Improving the learning experience in an undergraduate course on microbial metabolism by using an illustrated story.
citation: McKinlay JB, Kearns K. (2025). Improving the learning experience in an undergraduate course on microbial metabolism by using an illustrated story. Biochem Mol Biol Educ. https://doi.org/10.1002/bmb.21869
title: Minimal-integration illustrated hero's-journey story woven through an existing lecture sequence
description: The article describes a reusable course-level design: an illustrated story following a hero's-journey plotline, told in the third person to avoid anthropomorphizing E. coli, with each lecture opening with a few story slides before traditional lecture content. The implementation was deliberately minimal: "existing lectures were simply reordered to match the story chronology and story slides only took a few minutes from each lecture." The story was revisited across three course parts, exposing students to the full storyline multiple times.
requirements: A story plotline students find broadly familiar (the hero's journey)
Illustrated story materials and, optionally, an introductory video available before the course
constraints: A more extensive integration of a story into the course is possible but could require substantial effort, even with the materials available
target_learners: undergraduate life-science students in a microbial physiology and biochemistry lecture course
target_learning_goals: attitudes toward a detail-intensive science topic
functional knowledge of metabolism: applying details to specific situations
examples: In BIOL-M 350, the story followed an E. coli cell during a cholera outbreak, and lectures were organized around it with story slides opening each lecture and the whole storyline revisited in three course parts
key_sources: McKinlay JB, Kearns K. (2025). Improving the learning experience in an undergraduate course on microbial metabolism by using an illustrated story. Biochem Mol Biol Educ. https://doi.org/10.1002/bmb.21869

title: ILIAS open-source learning platform as the delivery infrastructure for RehAmpTT
description: The learning content was implemented on the Integrated Learning, Information and Work Cooperation System (ILIAS), the open-source learning platform of the Bundesarbeitsgemeinschaft digitale Lehre. The article notes that "The open-source software ILIAS is released under the GNU General Public License (GPL), so that it can be provided with content free of charge and likewise used free of charge by the general public." Technical bilingual implementation was carried out by staff of the Peter L. Reichertz Institute for Medical Informatics at MHH.
requirements: Technical support from medical-informatics staff for bilingual digitisation and placement of content in ILIAS
constraints: Data volume of images and videos was deliberately limited so the module can be used with poor internet connections
target_learners: medical professionals
amputees and relatives accessing the module online

examples: Content placed and designed in ILIAS by the two reviewers in close coordination with the informatics institute

article_title: Exploring the responses of preclinical medical students and professors to flipped learning for the development of clinical reasoning.
citation: Si Jihyun. (2024). Exploring the responses of preclinical medical students and professors to flipped learning for the development of clinical reasoning. Korean Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2024.297
title: Illness script worksheet adapted from Levin et al. for guiding preclinical clinical reasoning
description: The illness script worksheet is a process worksheet adapted from Levin et al. that "illustrate[s] illness-script-based reasoning processes and were used to guide the group discussions." It includes a clinical case vignette, initial problem representation, three possible differential diagnoses, and an illness script table for each, incorporating enabling conditions, pathophysiological faults, and consequences. Students completed it through group discussion and presented the results; assessment used rubrics.
requirements: Requires orientation covering worksheet examples and assessment rubrics, and a facilitator to guide group discussion
constraints: Adapted for preclinical students with minimal clinical reasoning training; original was used step-by-step with a facilitator per group
target_learners: preclinical second-year medical students
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning
differential diagnosis
illness script formation
examples: Students completed the worksheet through group discussions and each group presented their completed worksheets in class; the final test required completing two illness script worksheets

article_title: Fostering clinical reasoning ability in preclinical students through an illness script worksheet approach in flipped learning: a quasi-experimental study.
citation: Si Jihyun. (2024). Fostering clinical reasoning ability in preclinical students through an illness script worksheet approach in flipped learning: a quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05614-9
title: Illness script worksheet as recurring scaffolded group work with expert-completed cognitive feedback in flipped learning
description: A lesson-level design in which small groups complete a five-part illness script worksheet — "a clinical case vignette," initial problem representation, three ranked differential diagnoses with script tables, comparison and contrast, and a justified test list — during in-class flipped sessions. The worksheet is presented three times: as a completed example, as a guiding scaffold during group work, and as the professor's completed version for cognitive feedback by comparison after group presentations.
requirements: Professors develop clinical cases and upload reading materials and quizzes to an LMS one week before class
Groups of about six students with fixed membership and one facilitator managing multiple groups in one classroom
constraints: The article notes two-hour sessions created time constraints students identified as a weakness
The worksheet was modified from Levin et al.'s version, using the facilitators' version to include the comparison-and-contrast section
target_learners: preclinical second-year medical students
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning ability
illness script construction
differential diagnosis
examples: Over eight weeks and 17 two-hour classes, students worked through 15 clinical cases such as jaundice, hypotension, abdominal pain and diarrhea, completing worksheets as a group and presenting them for professor feedback
key_sources: Si Jihyun. (2024). Fostering clinical reasoning ability in preclinical students through an illness script worksheet approach in flipped learning: a quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05614-9

article_title: Evaluation the Effectiveness of Abridged IMNCI (7-Day) Course v Standard (11-Day) Course in Pakistan.
citation: Ariff Shabina, Sadiq Kamran, Jiwani Uswa, Ahmed Khalil, Nuzhat Khadija, Ahmed Shakeel, Nizami Qamruddin, Khan Iqtidar A., Ali Nabeela, Soofi Sajid Bashir, Bhutta Zulfiqar A. (2021). Evaluation the Effectiveness of Abridged IMNCI (7-Day) Course v Standard (11-Day) Course in Pakistan. Maternal and Child Health Journal. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10995-021-03276-3
title: When shortening standardized health-worker training, allocate time according to the needs of individual illnesses rather than cutting uniformly
description: A principle for abridging standardized training curricula: the authors observed that per-illness competence differed between course lengths and conclude that improving competency in the IMNCI approach for certain diseases "may require additional time and attention during the training", so any measures for shortening the training should take this factor into consideration rather than reducing time uniformly across content.
requirements: Abridged and standard courses must use the same teaching materials, tools, curriculum and training methodologies, differing only in time allocated to activities, so that outcome differences reflect time on task.
constraints: Proficiency in managing some illnesses (diarrhea, malaria, ARI, meningitis, malnutrition) was higher in the 11-day group, so uniform time reductions may not suit all content.
target_learners: Healthcare providers at first-level health facilities learning the IMNCI protocol, including doctors, nurses, midwives and lady health visitors
target_learning_goals: Assessment, classification and treatment of sick children according to the IMNCI protocol across multiple childhood illnesses
examples: The abridged course was only "redesigned and shortened in terms of the time allocated to each classroom activity and clinical practice session", with the same facilitators and materials for both groups.

article_title: The effectiveness of emergency knowledge training of pediatric medical workers based on the knowledge, skills, simulation model: a quasi-experimental study.
citation: Hu Yaojia, Zheng Bingya, Zhu Lihui, Tang Shuo, Lu Qi, Song Qingqing, Zhang Na, Zhong Yan. (2022). The effectiveness of emergency knowledge training of pediatric medical workers based on the knowledge, skills, simulation model: a quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03267-0
title: Self-designed emergency knowledge assessment questionnaire based on the 2019 ILCOR consensus, with 13 single-choice knowledge questions and an 8-item case analysis
description: The study used a self-designed questionnaire with 10 demographic questions and a first aid knowledge section based on the 2019 ILCOR consensus, containing 13 single-choice emergency knowledge questions and an emergency analysis case with 8 single-choice questions, scored out of 100 with a passing score of 60. Reliability testing showed "the internal consistency of the questionnaire was calculated to be 0.833 and the retest reliability was 0.899", with KMO = 0.889. Factor analysis identified factors of early identification, basic life support, and a multidimensional structure.
requirements: Review and approval by an evaluation committee and an ethics committee at the hospital
Validation by eight BLS and three ALS teachers and content evaluation by five CPR experts
constraints: The authors state that relying on questionnaire testing alone makes the data inherently limited, and reusing the same questionnaire pre and post may inflate second-test scores
target_learners: Hospital pediatric medical workers including nurses, doctors, and technicians
target_learning_goals: Assessment of emergency knowledge, case-analysis ability, and team cooperation in first aid
examples: The questionnaire was randomly distributed to 100 medical professionals during the trial phase using stratified random sampling, and analysis used SPSS version 24.0
